the Q377X mutation in Sox10 leads to a hypomorphic protein with very limited function, which is not sufficient to induce neurological defects, but that the presence of the protein in the nervous system may contribute to the development of pigmentation defects.
the human SOX mutation Q377X is not a dominant mutation in mice.
the human SOX mutation Q377X does not cause the phenotype that was postulated for it.

the analysis of the human SOXT0 Q377X mutation in mice and its consequences for genotype-phenotypic correlation.
the analysis of the human SOXA10 mutation Q377R in mice.
the analysis of the human SOXA10 mutation Q377 in a mouse model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SOX10 mutations can be divided into two groups.
SOX10 Q37X is not a disease-causing mutation but that it can be considered a hypomorphism with residual function.
SOX10 Q37X acts as a hypomorph in Schwann cells but as a null in oligodendroglial lineage cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SOX10 mutations are a necessary but not a sufficient cause for the phenotypes observed in SOX10 related disorders.
the presence of a mutant Sox10 allele is not sufficient to cause peripheral and central neuropathies, but that additional factors are required for this phenotype.

a SOX10 Q337X protein is unable to rescue the phenotypes of Sox10-deficient mice and that the presence of the mutant SOX10 in the mouse is sufficient for the manifestation of the Waardenburg syndrome and Hirschsprug disease phenotypes, but not the peripheral neuropathy and leukodystrophy phenotypes of PCWH patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence or absence of a SOX10 mutation in a patient's genome does not necessarily predict the severity of disease.
a heterozygous mutation that results in a mutant protein with residual function does not necessarily lead to disease.
the presence of a mutant protein in Schwanna cells and oligodengrocytes does not necessarily cause a disease.
